# Zymeworks (ZYME) — Event-Driven Special Situation Dossier

Prepared 2026-08-03. This is a catalyst underwrite, not a note on business quality. The
thesis is the gap between today's price and the value a pending regulatory decision
resolves to, bounded underneath by a floor made of cash and contracted cash flows.
Every load-bearing fact below was re-verified against primary sources today.

## The setup in one paragraph

Zymeworks is a Vancouver biotechnology company that has turned itself into something
closer to a royalty platform: it invents antibody drugs, licenses them to larger partners,
and collects milestones and royalties rather than building a sales force. Its lead
molecule, zanidatamab (sold as Ziihera), is a bispecific antibody — a single drug
engineered to grab the HER2 cancer target in two places at once. It is already approved
and selling in second-line HER2-positive biliary tract cancer through partner Jazz
Pharmaceuticals. The live catalyst is the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's decision on
widening that approval to first-line gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma — cancer of the
stomach and the junction where the esophagus meets it — which is a far larger patient
population. The decision carries a hard, scheduled date: a target action date (the
deadline by which the agency must rule) of August 25, 2026, twenty-two days from today.
Approval releases a $250 million cash payment to Zymeworks and opens a much bigger royalty
base. A rejection leaves the existing approval, the royalties, roughly $400 million of
cash and a newly bought respiratory franchise intact — which is what backstops the
downside near $18 a share.

## 1. Is the catalyst real, dated, and binding?

Yes on all three, and the evidence is first-party rather than press speculation.
Zymeworks' own first-quarter results release (May 7, 2026) states that the FDA accepted
Jazz's supplemental filing with Priority Review and set a target action date of
August 25, 2026, and that the agency has granted Breakthrough Therapy Designation to
zanidatamab combined with chemotherapy, with or without the immunotherapy TEVIMBRA, for
this indication. China's regulator has separately accepted the same filing. As of today,
no approval and no rejection letter has been announced by either Zymeworks or Jazz — the
event is genuinely still ahead of us, not already spent.

Three features make this a materially better-than-coin-flip binary. It is a label
expansion of a drug the agency has already approved and that a partner is already selling,
not a first-time approval. It carries both Priority Review and Breakthrough Therapy
Designation, which the FDA does not hand out against weak data. And it rests on a
completed Phase 3 trial in which the drug met its goals. The historical success rate for
efficacy supplements with that profile sits in the mid-to-high eighties as a percentage —
high, but not a certainty, and the residual is a real risk that must be priced.

## 2. Credibility of the parties

The regulatory filing and the eventual commercial launch belong to Jazz Pharmaceuticals, a
roughly $16 billion established commercial pharmaceutical company, not to Zymeworks. That
matters: the execution risk that usually sinks a small biotech at the approval line —
manufacturing readiness, sales infrastructure, regulatory correspondence — sits with a
partner that has done this repeatedly.

Zymeworks itself walks into the event fortified rather than desperate. Cash, equivalents
and marketable securities stood at $403.8 million as of March 31, 2026, up roughly 49%
from $270.6 million at the end of 2025. Management guides that this cash, plus the
anticipated milestones, funds operations beyond 2028. A company with a funded runway past
its catalyst is not a company that will be forced to sell stock into a bad outcome — the
classic way these situations turn a setback into a rout.

One genuine credibility mark in management's favour, and one against. In favour: they have
been buying their own stock in size, repurchasing 4.2 million shares under the 2025
programme at an average of $24.36 and utilising $95.8 million of a fresh $125 million
authorisation as of May 6, 2026. That average price sits above today's quote, so the
buying was not opportunistic bottom-fishing — it was conviction, and it has shrunk the
share count from about 73.0 million in May to roughly 71.6 million now. Against: the
first quarter was an ugly print, a loss of $0.59 a share against a consensus expecting
$0.10, as revenue fell away from prior-year milestone payments. That is the lumpy nature
of a milestone-driven model rather than a deterioration in the business, but it is a
reminder that reported earnings here tell you very little.

## 3. The verified downside floor

The $18 floor is not a chart level; it is built from assets that survive a rejection.

- **Cash.** Roughly $400 million as of the last report, about $5.50 a share against
  71.6 million shares.
- **The existing second-line approval.** Ziihera is approved and selling in biliary tract
  cancer today; that royalty and milestone stream is unaffected by a first-line decision.
- **Milestones that are not U.S.-dependent.** Management anticipates $440 million in total
  regulatory milestones across the United States, Europe, Japan and China for this
  indication. The $250 million U.S. payment is the largest single piece, but a U.S.
  rejection does not automatically forfeit the other jurisdictions — China's regulator has
  already accepted the filing.
- **The Yupelri franchise.** Via the pending Theravance purchase, Zymeworks acquires a 35%
  share of U.S. net profit on Yupelri, an inhaled treatment for chronic obstructive
  pulmonary disease. U.S. net sales were $266.6 million in 2025, growing 12%, throwing off
  roughly $60 million a year to Zymeworks, with generic protection licensed out to
  April 2039. There are a further $125 million of possible commercial milestones from
  partner Viatris and double-digit royalties on sales outside the United States.
- **The pipeline.** ZW191, an antibody-drug conjugate aimed at folate receptor alpha,
  showed a 78.6% confirmed response rate in the receptor-high group of platinum-resistant
  ovarian cancer patients at a June 2026 conference, with a median duration of response not
  yet reached. That is early-stage and unvalued here, but it is not nothing.

An $18 share price is about a $1.29 billion company. Set against roughly $400 million of
cash, a contracted respiratory annuity running to 2039, a live royalty stream and the
non-U.S. milestone slate, that is a defensible resting place rather than an optimistic one.

**The honest caveat on the floor.** This stock traded as low as $11.51 within the past
year. That was before Priority Review and before the Theravance deal, so the business
underneath is materially stronger now — but it demonstrates that this shareholder base will
sell well below fundamental value when a story breaks. The $18 figure is a value floor, not
a price floor; a rejection could easily overshoot through it for weeks before recovering.
Anyone sizing this must be able to sit through that.

## 4. The Theravance overlay — the merger tag, corrected

The catalyst board's tag suggests a merger arbitrage. That is misleading and worth
correcting precisely, because it changes what the risk actually is: Zymeworks is the buyer
here, not the target. There is no takeover premium to collect in this stock.

On June 29, 2026 Zymeworks agreed to acquire Theravance Biopharma for $17.00 a share in
cash, about $929 million, expected to close in the second half of 2026 subject to
regulatory clearance and a Theravance shareholder vote. The financing is the interesting
part and improves the floor rather than threatening it: $350 million of non-recourse debt
from OMERS Life Sciences secured solely against the U.S. Yupelri profit share, $219 million
of Zymeworks' own cash, and roughly $360 million of net cash sitting on Theravance's own
balance sheet, with a further $100 million milestone expected from Royalty Pharma in the
first quarter of 2027. Management describes the effective net investment as roughly halved.

Two things follow. First, the debt is non-recourse and ring-fenced to the acquired asset —
if Yupelri disappoints, the lender takes the asset, not the rest of Zymeworks. That is a
genuinely conservative structure, and it means this acquisition does not put the regulatory
thesis at risk. Second, Zymeworks only commits $219 million of its own cash, so the
post-deal balance sheet remains strong. The deal also carries roughly $2.5 billion of
Irish tax attributes, meaning future profits may be shielded from tax for a long time.

The market agrees the deal closes: Theravance trades at $16.86 against the $17.00 offer, a
gross spread of about 0.8%, which is where arbitrageurs price a transaction they regard as
near-certain. Deal-break risk is therefore small and should not be double-counted as a
worry.

## 5. Red flags scanned

Nothing solvency-shaped. There is no going-concern language, no maturity wall, no equity
overhang — the company is buying stock back rather than issuing it, and the only debt added
is non-recourse and secured against a separate asset. The specific risks that remain are
these, stated plainly:

- **The rejection tail.** A high probability of approval is not certainty. Roughly one time
  in seven, on the base rates, this goes the other way.
- **Date slippage.** The agency can extend a review, typically by three months. That defers
  the payoff rather than destroying it, but it would likely see the stock drift back toward
  the floor on impatience, and it would tie up capital longer than underwritten.
- **The earnings print in three days.** Zymeworks reports second-quarter results on
  August 6, 2026, and Jazz reports today, August 3. Either could carry commentary that
  moves the stock ahead of the decision. This is noise, not thesis, but it is noise
  arriving before the signal.
- **No dislocation cushion.** This is a well-covered $1.6 billion company with analysts
  carrying an average target above $40, not an abandoned orphan. The edge here is the
  probability of approval being better than the price implies — it is not a case of buying
  something nobody is looking at.

**Green flags:** insider-equivalent buying through a substantial repurchase programme at
prices above today's; cash up roughly half in a quarter; a partner-run regulatory process;
and a price that has drifted down into the event rather than run up into it.

## 6. The asymmetry

The stock closed at $21.94 on July 31, 2026, down 3.4% on the day and sitting below both
its 50-day average of $24.24 and its 200-day average of $23.98. It has, in other words,
been drifting lower into a dated catalyst — which is the opposite of the pattern that makes
event investing dangerous, where the market front-runs the news and leaves nothing on the
table.

Against a near-term event target of $27 and a floor of $18, the raw arithmetic is about
+23% upside against roughly -18% downside, a payoff ratio near 1.3 to 1. But the raw ratio
understates the case, because the two outcomes are not equally likely. Weighting the
outcomes at roughly 85% approval gives a probability-weighted value near $25.50, about 16%
above today's price, and the $27 target is itself conservative — the $250 million milestone
alone is about $3.49 a share of pure cash, before any re-rating of the royalty base for the
larger market, and the analyst community's average target sits at $40.50 with a range of
$31 to $48. Three brokers raised targets between late June and early July.

The essential point for a committee: the loss is bounded by assets you can count, the gain
is triggered by a date on the calendar, and the price has come to you in the fortnight
before that date.

interrogator_dossier:
# Zymeworks (ZYME) — Event Dossier

**Prepared 28 July 2026. All prices, dates and deal terms verified against live sources on
that date.**
**This updates the 27 July pass. Nothing in the thesis has broken; the decision date is now
28 days away rather than 29, the Phase 3 data has since been published in the New England
Journal of Medicine, and the share count and buyback figures are corrected to the company's
own disclosure (roughly 73.0 million shares, not 71.6 million).**

---

## 0. WHAT THIS NAME ACTUALLY IS

Zymeworks is a Vancouver-based biotechnology company that designs antibody-based cancer
drugs. The important thing to understand up front is that it does not sell its lead drug
itself. It invented zanidatamab — a bispecific antibody (one molecule that grabs two
different spots on the same cancer target at once) sold as Ziihera — and licensed the
commercial rights to Jazz Pharmaceuticals for the United States, Europe and Japan, and to
BeOne Medicines for Asia. Zymeworks collects milestone payments and royalties. It is, in
economic substance, a royalty holder with an early-stage research pipeline attached, not an
operating drug company.

That distinction governs everything below. The load-bearing event is a regulatory decision
on someone else's application, and the payout if it goes well is contractual and specific
rather than speculative.

**Live tape, 28 July 2026:** $23.00 per share; market value about $1.69 billion on roughly
73.0 million shares outstanding (company disclosure, 6 May 2026). The stock is 23% below its
52-week high of $29.75 and 100% above its 52-week low of $11.51 set in August 2025. It sits
below both its 50-day average of $24.42 and its 200-day average of $23.85, and it has drifted
down about 15% from $27.07 on 9 July — mildly oversold on ordinary volume, not washed out.

---

## 1. THE LOAD-BEARING EVENT: IS IT REAL, DATED, AND BINDING?

**Yes on all three, and this is the strongest part of the case.**

Jazz Pharmaceuticals submitted a supplemental biologics licence application (a request to
the United States Food and Drug Administration to add a new approved use to an
already-approved drug), asking to use Ziihera as a first-line treatment for HER2-positive
gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma — cancer of the stomach and the junction where the stomach
meets the oesophagus. The agency accepted the filing with Priority Review, which compresses
the review clock.

**The date is 25 August 2026.** That is the agency's target action date under the
Prescription Drug User Fee Act — the deadline by which it has committed to issue a decision.
It is 28 days from today. Zymeworks restated the date in its first-quarter results on 7 May
2026. I found no advisory-committee meeting scheduled, no denial letter, no extension and
no announced delay. An absent advisory committee is generally a favourable tell: the agency
convenes outside experts when it has doubts, and it did not convene one here.

**The evidence behind the application is strong and has now been peer-reviewed.** The
HERIZON-GEA-01 trial randomised 914 previously untreated patients across three arms and was
presented at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology gastrointestinal cancers
symposium. Zanidatamab-containing regimens beat the current standard of trastuzumab plus
chemotherapy on progression-free survival — how long patients live before the disease
worsens — at a median 12.4 months against 8.1 months, a hazard ratio of roughly 0.63 to 0.65.
The three-drug combination adding the immunotherapy tislelizumab delivered a statistically
significant overall-survival benefit, a median 26.4 months against 19.2 months, a hazard
ratio of 0.72. The full results have since been published in the New England Journal of
Medicine. The combination also carries Breakthrough Therapy designation, the agency's own
signal that it regards the advance as meaningful.

Crucially, this is a **label expansion on an already-marketed drug**, not a first approval.
Ziihera was approved in the United States in November 2024 for previously treated
HER2-positive biliary tract cancer, so its safety profile and manufacturing are established
and the question before the agency is breadth of use, not whether the molecule works. A
Phase 3 that hit both of its main goals, under Priority Review, with no advisory committee,
published in the leading journal in medicine, on a drug already on the market, is about as
clean a regulatory setup as this industry produces. **My working probability of approval on
or near the date is 85% to 90%.** The residual risk is the unglamorous kind: a manufacturing
or inspection finding at a third-party site, or a short administrative extension.

**What Zymeworks actually gets if it lands.** Under the Jazz agreement, Zymeworks is entitled
to a **$250 million regulatory milestone payment tied specifically to United States approval
in first-line gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma**. On roughly 73.0 million shares that is about
$3.42 per share of hard, non-dilutive cash. Beyond it sit further regulatory milestones for
European and Japanese approval in the same indication (part of an up-to-$525 million
regulatory tranche; management guides to up to $440 million of near-term regulatory
milestones in total), a $15 million milestone on Chinese approval from BeOne, up to $862.5
million of commercial milestones, and tiered royalties of 10% to 20% on Jazz's net sales.
The full agreement is worth up to about $1.76 billion.

---

## 2. THE ROYALTY HAS ALREADY BEEN PARTLY SOLD

An earlier pass on this name treated the March 2026 Royalty Pharma financing as an
unambiguous positive. It is not, and the distinction matters to the bull case.

On 2 March 2026 Zymeworks raised $250 million through a non-recourse royalty-backed note
from Royalty Pharma. That is real, non-dilutive money and it is why cash rose to $403.8
million by 31 March 2026 from $270.6 million at the end of 2025. But the repayment mechanism
is that **30% of the worldwide tiered royalties on Ziihera service the note**, leaving
Zymeworks with 70% until Royalty Pharma has collected 1.65 times the note by the end of 2033
(1.925 times thereafter), at which point full rights revert. The milestone payments are not
pledged and stay with Zymeworks in full.

In plain terms: the company has pre-sold roughly a third of the very royalty stream that
carries the upside case, and the interest is already running. Anyone valuing the zanidatamab
royalty must haircut it accordingly. This does not break the thesis — it caps it.

---

## 3. THE ACQUISITION, AND A MIS-TAGGED SETUP

Our watch-board tagged this name partly as a merger arbitrage. **That tag is wrong in
direction, and the error is material.** Zymeworks is the buyer, not the target. On 29 June
2026 it agreed to acquire Theravance Biopharma for $17.00 per share in cash, about $929
million, plus a contingent value right giving Theravance holders 80% of net proceeds from
monetising the drug ampreloxetine over ten years, a $50 million payment on first commercial
sale in one of six major markets, and a 10% sales royalty. Closing is targeted for the second
half of 2026 and requires antitrust clearance plus a two-thirds vote of Theravance holders;
the antitrust outside date is 28 December 2026, extendable twice by three months, with
reciprocal break fees of about $32.5 million.

There is no arbitrage spread for a Zymeworks holder to capture; the spread belongs to
Theravance shareholders. For Zymeworks this is a capital-allocation decision and must be
judged as one.

**Judged as one, it is financially clever and strategically odd.** The asset is YUPELRI
(revefenacin), the only approved nebulised long-acting muscarinic antagonist for maintenance
treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which did $266.6 million of United States
net sales in 2025, up 12%. Theravance holds a 35% profit share on it. The financing is well
engineered: a $350 million note from OMERS Life Sciences at 8.25% due 2036, secured *solely*
by the United States YUPELRI profit share, with 75% of that profit-share cash flow servicing
the debt and **no recourse to the rest of Zymeworks' balance sheet**; roughly $219 million of
Zymeworks' own cash; and roughly $360 million of net cash sitting on Theravance's balance
sheet at closing. **No Zymeworks shares are issued and no Zymeworks shareholder vote is
required.** Net capital at risk is about $219 million for a profitable commercial franchise
that arrives carrying more cash than was spent to buy it, plus an anticipated $100 million
TRELEGY milestone in the first quarter of 2027 and expected ongoing cash flow to Zymeworks of
roughly $60 million a year at the current run-rate.

Better still, Zymeworks agreed $17.00 against Theravance's prior close of about $17.63 — a
3.6% **discount** to the market price. Buying a public company below its trading price is
rare and signals a motivated seller.

**The market disliked it anyway.** Zymeworks fell about 5.6% on the announcement and has not
recovered it. The read is that investors saw an oncology company buying a respiratory
nebuliser business weeks before its own binary regulatory date and marked it down for lost
focus and execution risk rather than crediting the economics. I think the market has this
backwards, and it is the one genuine expectations gap in the name.

---

## 4. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR — WHAT ACTUALLY BACKSTOPS THE PRICE

This is where a special-situation investor should spend most of the scepticism, because the
floor is the only thing between you and a permanent loss. Here it is unusually well built —
and, importantly, it is built from assets rather than from an analyst's opinion.

**Plank one — cash. Real and large.** Cash, equivalents and marketable securities were
$403.8 million at 31 March 2026. Pro-forma for the acquisition — out roughly $219 million,
in roughly $360 million with Theravance, less a quarter of operating burn — the combined
company carries somewhere near $490 million to $545 million, about **$6.70 to $7.50 per
share**. Both large debts (the $250 million Royalty Pharma note and the $350 million OMERS
note) are non-recourse and serviced by specific asset cash flows, so neither can reach the
parent in a bad scenario. There is no covenant stress at the parent and no financing
contingency on the acquisition.

**Plank two — an already-approved product. Real.** The November 2024 approval in
previously-treated biliary tract cancer survives a rejection in gastroesophageal cancer
untouched, as does the existing royalty base, net of the 30% pledged to Royalty Pharma.

**Plank three — YUPELRI. Newly real, and the honest reason to like the Theravance deal.** A
$266.6 million-revenue commercial franchise throwing off a profit share is exactly what a
pre-profit biotechnology company has never had underneath it. It converts an abstract floor
into a cash-generating one. The caveat is that 75% of that cash flow is committed to the
OMERS note until repaid, so the near-term equity claim is thinner than the revenue line
suggests.

**Plank four — the wholly-owned pipeline. Optionality only.** ZW171, ZW191 (a folate
receptor alpha antibody-drug conjugate, which in July 2026 showed a 78.6% confirmed response
rate in receptor-positive platinum-resistant ovarian cancer patients) and ZW251 are early and
get marked near zero in a risk-off tape. Credit about $1 per share.

**Where the floor sits.** Strict asset math gives roughly $14 to $15 per share. But a
rejection would almost certainly be a fixable delay rather than a kill — the trial won on
both endpoints and is published — so the $250 million milestone would be deferred, not
destroyed. The trading floor therefore sits above the liquidation floor. Before the pivotal
data reached the market the stock traded in the $14 to $16 area, and it bottomed at $11.51 in
August 2025 when the outcome was genuinely unknown, which it no longer is. **I verify the
floor at approximately $18**, corroborating the board's figure, with the honest
acknowledgement that a genuine panic could briefly pierce it toward $15.

---

## 5. RED FLAGS

**Red flag one — much of the approval is already in the price.** The stock doubled off its
August 2025 low on the pivotal data. Work the arithmetic backwards: with an $18 floor and
87% approval odds, the market's implied approval-case value is only about $23.75, barely
above spot. Either the market is pricing worse odds than the evidence supports, or it is
pricing a smaller win. Either way, what you are buying is favourable odds at a fair price,
not a screaming mispricing.

**Red flag two — the royalty upside is capped** by the Royalty Pharma pledge described above.

**Red flag three — Zymeworks controls none of the commercial outcome.** Jazz files, Jazz
launches, Jazz books the sales that drive the royalty. A slow launch against entrenched
trastuzumab prescribing is not something this management can fix, and Zymeworks cannot repair
a problem in an application it does not own.

**Red flag four — a communication vacuum into the event.** Second-quarter results land on 6
August 2026 and the company has said it will **not** host a conference call, because of the
pending acquisition. That removes the last opportunity for management to frame the story
before the agency acts.

**Red flag five — acquisition timing and coherence.** Committing $219 million of cash and
management bandwidth to a respiratory purchase eight weeks before a binary regulatory
decision is a discipline question, however good the engineering. An oncology platform now
owns a product whose generic entry is settled for April 2039.

**Red flag six — the loss run.** First-quarter 2026 revenue fell to $2.4 million from $27.1
million a year earlier, on the absence of prior-year one-off milestones, with a $44.2 million
net loss — a reminder that reported revenue in a milestone business is lumpy and nearly
meaningless quarter to quarter. Operating expenses were controlled: $34.5 million of research
and development and $15.1 million of general and administrative, against three-year guidance
of roughly $300 million of adjusted gross operating expense for 2026 to 2028.

**Red flag seven — crowded expectations.** The sell side is close to unanimous, with targets
clustered in the high thirties to low forties (Truist raised to $31 on 7 July 2026; Wells
Fargo and Citi around $37; Stifel $47). When everyone is positive, a rejection moves the
price more than an approval does.

**What I checked and did not find:** no going-concern language, no equity or convertible
issuance funding the deal, no covenant stress at the parent, no financing contingency, and no
antitrust second request — a cash purchase of a respiratory asset by an oncology company
raises no overlap.

---

## 6. GREEN FLAGS

**Green flag one — a contractual, dated, non-discretionary payout.** The $250 million is not
a re-rating hope; it is a contract term triggered by a named regulatory action on a named
date. That is rarer and better than most setups on our board.

**Green flag two — clean, published data on a drug already on the market.** Both main
endpoints met across 914 patients, priority review, no advisory committee, New England
